# Capstone Brief and Rubric {#sec-capstone-brief}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Appendix status: drafted.** Everything needed to scope, build and submit the
capstone. Read alongside @sec-capstone, which walks one worked example end to
end and is the model for the reasoning this brief asks for.
:::

## Scope {#sec-capstone-brief-scope}

**The one hard requirement: a working agent that calls at least one real tool.**
Real means it reaches something outside the model — an API, a database, a file
system, a search index. A tool that returns a hard-coded string is a mock, and a
project built on mocks cannot demonstrate the thing this course is about.

Everything else is negotiable, and smaller is better. [One task done properly
beats three demonstrated.]{.hl}

**Explicit non-goals**, because over-scoping is the single most common way a
capstone fails:

- **You are not training a model.** Fine-tuning is allowed and never required.
  No marks are attached to it.
- **You are not building a product.** No authentication, no deployment, no user
  interface beyond what you need to demonstrate the system.
- **You are not expected to beat a benchmark.** A measured negative result,
  honestly reported, scores as well as a positive one.
- **You are not writing a survey.** The deliverable is a system and an argument
  about it, not a literature review.

**Team size** is one to three. Solo projects are allowed and are graded on the
same rubric with the same expectations — the scope should shrink accordingly,
and shrinking it is your decision to make and to justify.

## Deliverables {#sec-capstone-brief-deliverables}

Four artefacts, submitted as one repository plus a short demo.

**1. The repository.** A layout that someone else can run:

```text
  README.md          what it does, how to run it, what it needs
  src/               the system
  evals/             the eval set and the harness that runs it
  report.md          the written argument (below)
  requirements.txt   or equivalent, with versions pinned
```

**2. The evaluation harness.** This is not optional and it is not a test suite
for your code. It is a set of cases with known answers, a scorer, and a script
that runs them and prints a number (@sec-agent-eval, @sec-production-eval).
Twenty to fifty items is enough. Ship it alongside the system, not afterwards.

**3. The report.** Three to five pages, and its structure is the rubric below:
what problem, what you built and what you rejected, what you measured, what it
says, and what you would do next. Include your non-goals.

**4. The demo.** Ten minutes: the system doing the thing, one failure case, and
your headline number. Live or recorded — recorded is safer and equally
acceptable.

## Rubric {#sec-capstone-brief-rubric}

[Non-CS students are graded on reasoning, not on code elegance.]{.hl} A clear
argument for a simple system, with a measurement that could have refuted it,
beats an elaborate system nobody can evaluate.

| axis | weight | what full marks look like |
|:--|--:|:--|
| **Problem framing** | 15% | The task is stated precisely enough to be wrong. Non-goals are written down. You can say who would use this and what they would do instead. |
| **Data and ground truth** | 20% | You can say where every item came from and how you know its correct answer. Annotation disagreement is measured, not assumed away (@sec-data-annotation). |
| **Evaluation design** | 25% | A real eval set, a scorer you validated on a known-answer input, a baseline to compare against, and uncertainty reported (@sec-llm-eval). |
| **Engineering** | 20% | It runs from the README on a machine that is not yours. Tools are real. Failure modes are handled rather than hidden. |
| **Write-up** | 20% | The argument is followable, the claims match the evidence, and the negative results are in there. |

: Capstone rubric {tbl-colwidths="[24,10,66]"}

Four things that cost marks disproportionately, all of them avoidable:

- **A metric nobody validated.** Feed your scorer a perfect prediction and
  confirm it returns a perfect score. @sec-turkish-nlp is a chapter's worth of
  reasons.
- **A claim without an interval.** "Our agent resolves 80% of tickets" needs a
  set size and a definition of resolved.
- **No baseline.** Compared against nothing, any number is unreadable. A
  majority-class floor or a keyword rule takes an hour.
- **A demo instead of a measurement.** Three impressive examples is an anecdote.

Two things that earn marks more than students expect: **reporting what did not
work**, and **finding a bug in your own instrument**. Both are the behaviour the
whole book argues for.

## Timeline {#sec-capstone-brief-timeline}

Anchored to the week numbers in @sec-syllabus so the appendix survives a change
of semester.

| when | what is due | what it should contain |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Week 5** | Proposal, one page | The task, the tool you will call, where ground truth comes from, and your non-goals |
| **Week 8** | Eval set, submitted | Twenty items minimum with known answers, plus the scorer, plus evidence you validated the scorer |
| **Week 11** | Mid-point check-in | A working end-to-end path, however crude, and a first number |
| **Week 14** | Repository, report, demo | Everything above |

: Capstone milestones {tbl-colwidths="[14,26,60]"}

The week-8 deadline is deliberately before most systems work. [Writing the eval
before the system is the single strongest predictor of a capstone that goes
well]{.hl}, and it is the habit @sec-capstone argues for at production scale.

## Project shapes that work {#sec-capstone-brief-past}

Anonymised, and described by shape rather than by result so you can see whether
yours rhymes with one.

**A support agent over a real document set.** Retrieval over a company's own
policy PDFs, one lookup tool, evaluated on questions written by someone who
knew the answers. Worked because the ground truth existed before the system did.

**A structured-extraction pipeline for Turkish forms.** Invoices to JSON, scored
per field against hand-checked values. Worked because per-field scoring showed
*which* field was failing, which is the difference between a number and a
finding.

**A literature triage agent.** Given a research question, search, filter,
summarise. Worked because the student measured retrieval separately from
summarisation and could say which half was the problem.

**A code-review assistant on a real repository.** Worked because the baseline —
a linter — was honest and hard to beat, and the report said where it was not
beaten.

And two shapes that did not work, with the reason:

**A multi-agent system with five roles**, none of which could be evaluated
separately. There was no way to tell whether the orchestration helped, because
there was nothing to compare it against.

**A chatbot with no eval set**, demonstrated on examples chosen after the fact.
The system may well have been good; nothing in the submission could establish
it.

Both failed the same way, and it is the failure this book was written against:
[a system nobody can measure is a system nobody can improve, defend, or
trust.]{.hl}
